title: kv-garbage-mark-and-sweep-latency-exploration
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an exploratory investigation into a mark-and-sweep inspired eviction pass (we call it 'KV-garbage') and how it interacts with long-tail reuse, KV paging, and memory bandwidth on our typical inference stacks. Goal: understand whether periodic sweep passes can reduce tail-latency by avoiding large eviction storms and whether the cost (extra memory scans / bw) outweighs the gains for common serving workloads.

Background / motivating signal:
- Multiple recent incidents showed >99th percentile tail spikes correlated with periodic heavy-spill events when GC-like cleanup and spilling coincided with bursty inference traffic.
- Existing LRU-like heuristics work well for steady-state reuse but struggle when ephemeral hotwindows shift quickly; eviction cascades to NVMe cause synchronous IO bursts.
- Hypothesis: a coordinated lightweight mark-and-sweep that preemptively identifies stale pages and performs low-priority reclamation (spillback) could flatten tail spikes by de-synchronising evictions from critical request paths.

High-level design (prototype):
- Mark phase: sample active resident set via async per-bank touch logging over a 1s sliding window (hardware-friendly bitmap sample, 1/128 sampling rate).
- Sweep phase: background thread iterates candidate page list per-NUMA bank and issues low-priority writebacks or demotions to SSD with rate limiter tied to measured memory bandwidth headroom.
- Resurrection handling: re-promotion allowed; pages kept in a thin sticky-cache for quick recovery (TTL 200ms) before full eviction.
- Safety: background sweep yields to foreground prefetches and respects QoS signals (latency SLO flags from request tracer).

Hypotheses to test:
1) Preemptive sweep reduces 99.9th percentile token latency during heavy mixed workloads by smoothing NVMe burst IO.
2) Background scans introduce measurable extra DRAM bandwidth usage but can be gated to keep net cost < 5% throughput loss.
3) Sticky-cache TTL is critical: too long -> wasted residency, too short -> re-promotion storm.

Experiment matrix:
- Baselines: current LRU eviction (production config), LRU + periodic aggressive eviction (control), LRU + KV-garbage with three sweep rates (low/med/high) and three TTLs (50ms/200ms/1s).
- Workloads: (A) chat-embedding mix (many short sequences, high reuse), (B) long-context summarization (few long sequences), (C) synthetic bursty mix with hotkey surges (95/5 skew), (D) realistic production trace replay for a 12hr window sampled from regional cluster.
- Metrics: token tail latency (p50/p95/p99/p99.9), NVMe IO QPS and burstiness (peak QPS over 1s), DRAM measured bandwidth delta (per-socket), re-promotion rate (resurrects/sec), effective hit-rate, per-request CPU offload cost.

Microbench harness and knobs used:
- Kernel: linux-6.1 with io_uring for spillback path, perf counters on mem_bandwidth (Intel RAPL-style counters and GPU-device DMA meters where applicable).
- Sampling probe: /proc/pagemap + hardware ASID sampling disabled to avoid jitter; we used a lightweight shadow bitmap in userspace communicated via ring buffer to background sweeper.
- Rate limiter: token-bucket using adaptive headroom = max(0, memory_bw_budget - current_stream_bw).

Results summary (selected):
- Workload A (high reuse): KV-garbage low sweep reduced p99.9 by ~22% vs baseline; DRAM bandwidth increased by 3% (acceptable). TTL=200ms hit best tradeoff: re-promotion ~12/s.
- Workload B (long sequences): negligible benefit; sweep did not reduce tail because paging dominated by long KV footprints — sweep occasionally increased latency when high sweep concurrency was used.
- Workload C (hotkey surges): medium sweep rate with short TTL (50ms) reduced NVMe peak QPS by ~38% and p99 improved 15%, but re-promotion rate shot up (relatively high CPU churn).
- Trace replay: overall p99.9 improved 9% with medium sweep + TTL 200ms; DRAM bw delta averaged +4.6% across nodes.

Detailed observations / anomalies:
- Bandwidth coupling: we saw that background sweep competes with prefetch threads for memory channels leading to small increases in CPU-request latencies when sweeper was not bank-aware. Adding per-bank pacing removed that regression.
- Sticky-cache undersizing: when sticky-cache memory fraction < 0.5% of resident set, re-promotion storms were common. Sizing to 1% removed most churn.
- Sweep granularity: fine-grained page scanning (4KB pages) had much higher overhead than 64KB-aligned cluster scans; cluster scans retained eviction candidate fidelity while reducing traversal cost by ~3.8x.
- Adverse interaction with NVMe QoS: on platforms where NVMe scheduler limited background IO, sweep threads flooded IO queues and caused prioritisation inversion. Fixing with IO classifiable priority avoids it.

Quantitative tables (high level):
- p99.9 change vs baseline (workload A/B/C/trace): -22% / +3% / -15% / -9%
- DRAM bw delta (avg): +3% / +1% / +5% / +4.6%
- NVMe peak reduction (where applicable): 0% / 0% / 38% / 22%
- Re-promotion cost (CPU cycles per second): low/med/high sweeps -> 5%/12%/26% CPU overhead on housekeeping thread.

Conclusions / recommendations:
- KV-garbage (mark-and-sweep style background reclamation) shows promise for mixed workloads where eviction storms cause NVMe burst IO. It is not universally beneficial: long-sequence dominated workloads see little gain and can regress if sweeps are not bank-aware or IO-priority-safe.
- Operational defaults to consider: medium sweep rate + sticky-cache=1% of resident set + cluster-scan size 64KB + bank-aware pacing + IO priority class for background spills. This config gave consistent tail wins with <5% DRAM bandwidth and ~12% CPU householding cost.
- Feature flag + dynamic auto-tuner: enable KV-garbage only when telemetry indicates imminent spillback (resident occupancy growth rate > threshold) or detected spike in NVMe QPS. An auto-tuner should select TTL and sweep rate based on observed re-promotion ratio.

Next experiments / open questions:
- Evaluate on dedicated nodes with different NVMe QoS profiles (QAT-enabled hardware, slow consumer-grade NVMe) to test robustness.
- Better sampling: hardware-assisted tagged sampling to reduce background traversal cost further.
- Formalize cost model: build a simple econometric model mapping sweep rate -> bandwidth cost -> tail latency benefit to drive autoscaling policy.
- Integration with routing: can we pre-warm alternative model variants to reduce need for urgent promotions during hot surges?

Action items:
- Prototype branch: PR 2713 contains the initial sweeper + sticky-cache implementation (owners: Liam Chen, Asha Patel). Run perf harness across region-b1 cluster next week. (owner: Liam Chen)
- Add per-bank pacing and IO-class prioritizer to sweep path (owner: María González)
- Create dashboard: KV-garbage health (sweep rate, re-promotions, NVMe QPS, bw delta) and auto-tuner signals (owner: Noah Brooks)

Appendix - quick commands / traces used:
- Reproducer harness (synthetic): ./tools/kv-replay --trace traces/hotkey-burst-20250801.json --sweep-config {rate=medium,ttl=200ms}
- Perf counters: sudo perf stat -e LLC-loads,LLC-store-misses,mem_load_uops_retired:all -a sleep 60
- NVMe QPS sampling: watch -n1 'cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/stat | awk "{print $4}"'

Notes to reviewers: this is exploratory; results vary by CPU microarchitecture, PCIe gen, and NVMe firmware. Recommend running the medium-sweep default in a small canary pool before wider rollout.
